messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 27
- Gender: Non-binary
- Ethnicity: Oceania
- Relationship Status: In a relationship
- Occupation: Special Education Teacher
- Trauma Type: Stalking
- Pcl5: 34

**Vignette: Aroha, Age 27**

Aroha grew up on the outskirts of Auckland, the youngest of four siblings in a large Māori family where the front door was rarely locked and neighbors moved through the house as freely as relatives. That sense of open, easy safety felt like a birthright — until about two years ago, when a former classmate from their undergraduate teaching program began showing up in places where Aroha had no reason to expect them.

It started quietly enough. A few too many comments on social media posts. A text message that referenced something Aroha had mentioned only in passing, weeks earlier. Then the classmate appeared at the café where Aroha spent Sunday mornings grading lesson plans. Then outside the school where Aroha had recently taken a position teaching students with complex learning needs. Each encounter was framed as coincidence, offered with a smile that Aroha felt in their chest long after the person had gone. Over the following four months, the pattern intensified — notes left on Aroha's car, a bouquet delivered to the school front office, and eventually a series of messages that made explicit what Aroha had already understood in their body: this person was watching them, and had been for some time.

The formal intervention — a police report, a restraining order, the classmate eventually relocating — resolved the external situation. What it did not resolve was the architecture of fear that had quietly rebuilt itself inside Aroha during those months.

Now, two years on, Aroha moves through the world with a vigilance that exhausts them. Walking from the school car park to the building each morning, they scan faces, read postures, catalogue exits. They have rearranged their classroom so that their desk faces the door. Students and colleagues experience Aroha as warm and attentive — and Aroha genuinely loves the work, the particular intimacy of helping a child find a way into learning that fits the shape of their mind — but maintaining that presence costs something. By the time Aroha arrives home to their partner, Sione, there is very little left.

Sleep is thin and unreliable. Aroha wakes most nights between two and four in the morning with a heart rate that belongs to someone running, though they are lying still. The dreams are not always dramatic — sometimes it is simply the feeling of being observed, a pressure at the back of the neck, and then waking into a dark room that takes several seconds to recognize as safe. Aroha has stopped telling Sione about the dreams as often, not wanting to wear out the concern they can see in his face.

There are stretches of the day when Aroha feels hollowed out, as though the emotional range has been narrowed without their consent. They notice this most acutely when a student achieves something meaningful — a breakthrough with a child who has been struggling to communicate — and the joy Aroha expects to feel arrives muted, like a sound heard through a closed door. This troubles them perhaps more than the nightmares do. Teaching was supposed to be the thing that stayed whole.

Aroha has become selective about social plans, canceling more often than not when gatherings involve unfamiliar venues or crowds. They have not returned to the café where they used to grade on Sundays. The route they take to work changes regularly, a habit that began as a practical precaution and has since become compulsive — they feel genuinely uneasy on the days when circumstance forces them to drive the same road twice in a row.

What Aroha finds hardest to articulate, even to Sione, is that the threat is gone and the fear is not. The restraining order is real. The classmate is in another city. Aroha knows this. And yet the body has not received the news, or has received it and chosen not to believe it — holding its breath, watching the door, waiting for the coincidence that proves it was right all along.
